native_result.query: How does the prevalence of non-native plants introduced via gardening vary based on habitat type?
native_result.HypoA: The prevalence of gardening-introduced non-native plants differs between urban/cropland habitats and natural habitats.
native_result.HypoB: The prevalence of non-native plants introduced via gardening is strongly habitat-dependent and concentrated in a subset of habitats. Among invaded plots, gardening-introduced species make up the largest share of the non-native assemblage in wetlands (0.65), coastal (0.53) and riparian (0.44) habitats, are a moderate minority in urban (0.29) and cropland (0.17) plots, and are entirely absent from rock outcrops (0). In absolute terms the concentration is even sharper: 78% of all gardening occurrences (132/169) fall in just four habitats (urban 45, riparian 35, wetlands 29, coastal 23), while rock outcrops, scrublands, meadows and broad-leaved forests together hold only ~6%. Gardening-derived non-natives are therefore most prevalent in human-modified and water-associated habitats (urban, riparian, wetland, coastal) and rare to absent in native forest, scrubland and rock-outcrop habitats.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded invaded_niche_pathways.csv (632x37, 0 missing) as the habitat axis (10 habitat types); computed per-habitat mean n.gard, total n.gard, share of empty plots, and bootstrapped 95% CI on the per-plot share n.gard/n.total restricted to invaded plots (n.total>0). Fitted a negative-binomial GLM n.gard ~ habitat + offset(log n.total) with Scrublands as reference to obtain incidence-rate ratios. Ran Kruskal-Wallis and chi-square robustness checks. Cross-checked with species-level invasion_success_pathways.csv (81 species) comparing mean habitat.range by intro.pathway (3 duplicated=TRUE gardening rows kept).
